newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military not mired in Cold War - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military not mired in Cold War - Cohen.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen denied to a key Senate committee on Tuesday that the U.S. military was mired in outdated Cold War strategy and refusing to reshape itself for the 21st Century.

Members of the Senate Armed Services Committee questioned a new Pentagon plan submitted this week which calls for only small troop cuts and little change in defence posture by the turn of the century despite the collapse of the Soviet Union.

But pointing to North Korea, Iraq and Iran, Cohen bridled at suggestions that the the United States should cut its armed forces more deeply and perhaps even scrap its costly strategy of being prepared to fight two major regional wars at once.

"With respect to the charge that this is simply Cold War thinking, let me indicate to you that I think that the charge is without merit," Cohen said. He noted that the military had already cut troop levels by one third to a current 1.4 million since 1985.
"We have to deal with the world as it exists today unless we're willing to take greater risks," he told senators.

"We cannot dismiss the threat that North Korea poses. We can't dismiss (Iraq's President) Saddam Hussein in terms of what kind of threat he poses to that region. We cannot ignore the potential threat of Iran to the stability of the region itself."

Cohen on Monday unveiled the new quadrennial defence review, pressing Congress to okay two more rounds of domestic military base closings to save money for high-tech arms, while paring only 61,700 troops from the current armed forces.

Despite some criticism of the plan, however, several senators on the committee, including Republican John McCain of Arizona, praised Cohen for having the "courage" to recommend two new rounds of politically-unpopular base closings in 1999 and 2001.
"I hope that this committee will authorise another round of base closings -- or two," said McCain.

Cohen said that he realised that many members of Congress feared the politically-explosive subject of more base closings following four recent rounds of downsizing that have shut 98 major facilities in the United States.
"And if you decide it's not politically possible, it's not popular, it's not acceptable, it's not necessary, then obviously we have to live with that," he testified.
"But there are also consequences that flow from that."
Cohen said that Congress must both close additional bases and allow the Pentagon to turn over the maintenance of many weapons and military facilities to private contractors to save money.
